          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

SecurityEvent

| where Account !endswith "$"

ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Kratos PhaaS network/DNS egress to phishing domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142 · [LLM] Inbound email with URL to Kratos phishing domain clicked via Safe Links · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kratos phishing kit web-asset fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg / PTT-SOft path) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kratos PhaaS credential-exfil POST to next.php / save.php on phishing host · [LLM] Microsoft 365 successful sign-in sourced from Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142
Kratos PhaaS network/DNS egress to phishing domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter contact with the seized Kratos phishing-as-a-service domains and the Egyptian operator IP 41.128.0.142. Article-specific because it keys on the exact domain set and shared operator IP tied to the fake Microsoft 365 login infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the article's exact seized Kratos domain set plus operator IP 41.128.0.142, both confirmed by ANY.RUN's Kratos write-up which maps them to the fake M365 login infrastructure. IOC-anchored, so FP is essentially limited to sinkhole/researcher traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure • https://www.presseportal.de/blaulicht/pm/7/6318131
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel/sinkhole crawlers hosted in the environment resolving the domains
  • A .de/.es compromised-but-legitimate WordPress site (e.g. crm-technik.de) being visited for benign reasons after cleanup
  • URL-scanning email gateway or Safe Links backend detonation traffic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("safelinks","urldetonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved or connected, pull the InitiatingProcess (expect a browser) and confirm it was a real user session vs. a scanner. 2) Contain: if a real user reached a fake M365 page, force an Entra ID password reset AND revoke all sessions/refresh tokens (password reset alone is insufficient — Kratos steals session cookies), block the domains/IP at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user for anomalous sign-ins, new inbox rules, and OAuth grants; check other hosts for the same domain/IP contact.

Kratos phishing kit web-asset fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg / PTT-SOft path) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Kratos kit's static-asset fingerprint: a browser session requesting both /assets/img/barr.svg and /assets/img/lg.svg (or the /PTT/SOft/ path, or dsa.svg+sid.gif), which ANY.RUN reports as ~90% recall with near-zero FPs for the fake Microsoft 365 login page. Article-specific because these asset paths and their content hashes are unique to the Kratos kit. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's V1 fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg in one session, ~90% recall), V0 (/PTT/SOft/) and V2 (dsa.svg + sid.gif); the assets' content hashes (barr.svg 949895df..., lg.svg cd231b89..., styles.css c447e75f..., ani.gif 9d1a1a5e...) are the article's SHA256 IOCs, confirming the kit. Requiring the asset pair, not a single generic file, keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://gbhackers.com/kratos-phaas-targets-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign site coincidentally serving files named lg.svg and barr.svg in the same 5-minute window (rare; the pair is the discriminator)
  • Safe Links / URL-scanner backend detonating the phishing page
  • Analyst re-detonating the URL during triage
  • Web-archive / cache proxy replaying the captured page
Suppression filter
| where Requests > 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting host+user actually rendered the page (both assets present) vs. a scanner; capture the parent domain hosting the assets. 2) Contain: treat as credential theft — force password reset and revoke Entra ID sessions/tokens for the user, block the host domain at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: search Entra sign-ins for that user from new IPs (especially 41.128.0.142), review new inbox forwarding rules and OAuth consents, and sweep other hosts for the same asset fingerprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("barr.svg","lg.svg","dsa.svg","sid.gif","imag.jpg","/PTT/SOft/") | extend Asset=case(RemoteUrl has "barr.svg","barr.svg", RemoteUrl has "lg.svg","lg.svg", RemoteUrl has "dsa.svg","dsa.svg", RemoteUrl has "sid.gif","sid.gif", RemoteUrl has "imag.jpg","imag.jpg","ptt") | summarize Assets=make_set(Asset), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl), Requests=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m) | where (set_has_element(Assets,"barr.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"lg.svg")) or set_has_element(Assets,"ptt") or (set_has_element(Assets,"dsa.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"sid.gif")) | order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any ("barr.svg","lg.svg","dsa.svg","sid.gif","imag.jpg","/PTT/SOft/") | extend Asset=case(Url has "barr.svg","barr.svg", Url has "lg.svg","lg.svg", Url has "dsa.svg","dsa.svg", Url has "sid.gif","sid.gif", Url has "imag.jpg","imag.jpg","ptt") | summarize Assets=make_set(Asset), Urls=make_set(Url) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | where (set_has_element(Assets,"barr.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"lg.svg")) or set_has_element(Assets,"ptt") or (set_has_element(Assets,"dsa.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"sid.gif")) | order by TimeGenerated desc

Kratos PhaaS credential-exfil POST to next.php / save.php on phishing host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-harvesting HTTP POST from a victim browser to the Kratos exfil endpoints (/next.php, /nex.php, /n3xt.php, /save.php, /SOft/mini.php) on a known Kratos domain or the operator IP. Article-specific because it pairs the kit's exact exfil filenames with the seized infrastructure, indicating credentials were actually submitted. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's documented Kratos exfil endpoints (next.php / nex.php / n3xt.php / save.php / SOft/mini.php with POST params di,pr) anchored to the article's seized domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142, so a match means credentials were actually POSTed — a confirmed-victim signal, not just a page view. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1056.003 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app on a compromised .de/.es host using next.php/save.php naming (mitigated by requiring the Kratos domain/IP)
  • Researcher submitting decoy credentials during triage
  • Automated form-fuzzing / DAST scanner hitting the phishing host
  • Safe Links backend detonation submitting a synthetic credential
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the POST originated from a real user browser session and identify the account; treat any TRUE match as a credential-compromise event. 2) Contain: immediately reset the user's Entra ID password and revoke all sessions and refresh tokens (Kratos steals cookies/tokens — reset alone is insufficient), enforce MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs for that account from 41.128.0.142 and other new IPs, check for newly created inbox rules, mail-forwarding, OAuth app consents, and outbound BEC-themed mail to the user's contacts.

Inbound email with URL to Kratos phishing domain clicked via Safe Links AIDelivery High
Correlates delivered inbound email carrying a URL to a Kratos phishing domain with a subsequent Safe Links click by the recipient. Article-specific because it filters on the exact seized Kratos domain set rather than generic phishing heuristics, and flags the click-through that turns delivery into likely compromise. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact seized Kratos domains in delivered inbound email URLs, then joins Safe Links click telemetry to prioritise recipients who actually clicked — high fidelity because the domain set is the IOC and the click makes credential submission likely. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Kratos domain that was a compromised-but-legitimate site (e.g. crm-technik.de) also sending benign mail before compromise
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaign reusing a since-seized domain
  • Threat-intel newsletter or IR report email quoting the domain as text (URL present but benign context)
  • Analyst forwarding the phishing sample internally for review
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","External")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message was Delivered (not Blocked/Junked) and whether UrlClickEvents shows a click; prioritise ClickedThrough recipients. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide (ZAP), reset password + revoke sessions/tokens for any recipient who clicked, and block the sender + domains. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/cluster, check clicked users' sign-ins from 41.128.0.142, and review for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.

// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let D=dynamic(["dwbud.vilaribit.com","razen.online","theoceanac.online","jumpast.es","enerdizerandtron.de","abal.my","starwellmedia.com","aabiz.de","aspireglobal.ltd","buenne.de","dufllot.sbs","espaciocf.de","ihrsupportcenter.de","ilersls.org","aaalen.de","rundwasser.de","smartcontrolengineer.com","sonnenbrillenspot.de","trisrnareprjdocz.com","crm-technik.de"]); let Clicks = UrlClickEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough") | where Url has_any (D) | project ClickTime=TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, ClickedUrl=Url, NetworkMessageId, IsClickedThrough; EmailEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" | join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | where UrlDomain has_any (D) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId | join kind=leftouter Clicks on NetworkMessageId | project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, UrlDomain, Url, ClickTime, IsClickedThrough | order by TimeGenerated desc
Microsoft 365 successful sign-in sourced from Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on any successful Entra ID / M365 sign-in whose source IP is the Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142, indicating an operator replaying stolen credentials or session tokens for account takeover. Article-specific because it keys on the single operator IP tied to the seized Kratos backend. Rationale: 41.128.0.142 is the Kratos operator IP (Egypt) confirmed by ANY.RUN; any successful M365 sign-in from it is near-certain account takeover, so it is a clean single-IOC alerting rule with essentially zero legitimate FP. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A traveler or VPN egress genuinely using 41.128.0.142 (unlikely — it is dedicated operator infrastructure)
  • Threat-intel enrichment or a red-team exercise deliberately authenticating from that IP
  • Shared NAT if the operator IP were ever reassigned by the hosting provider after seizure
  • Security tooling health-check logins pinned to that address (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and capture the account, app, and conditional-access outcome. 2) Contain: disable the account or force sign-out, reset password AND revoke all refresh/session tokens, require MFA re-registration; block 41.128.0.142 in Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts that authenticated from this IP, review each for new inbox rules, mail forwarding, OAuth consents, mass mailbox reads, and outbound BEC mail to contacts.
AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where IPAddress == "41.128.0.142" | where ErrorCode == 0 | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn | order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress == "41.128.0.142" | where ResultType == 0 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState | order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c9d1a3b5-7e2f-4a6c-8b13-2d5f9e0c4a17
status: experimental
description: Detects a successful Entra ID sign-in sourced from the Kratos phishing-as-a-service operator IP 41.128.0.142, indicating credential/session-token replay and account takeover.

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22
tags:

    - attack.t1539
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: signinlogs
detection:
    selection:
        IPAddress: '41.128.0.142'
        ResultType: 0
    condition: selection
level: high
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 CIDR(@network.client.ip, 41.128.0.142/32)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" AND Authentication.src="41.128.0.142" by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" AND Authentication.src="41.128.0.142" by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SmartLoader: renamed LuaJIT interpreter launched with .txt/.log data-file stage AIInstallation High
Hunts the SmartLoader execution signature where a batch launcher runs a LuaJIT interpreter (often renamed) passing an obfuscated Lua payload disguised as a text/log/json file (e.g. `start luajit.exe tcp.log`, `vm_s390x.exe lib_bit.txt`). This is the core FakeGit loader trigger and is highly specific to the observed binary+argument pairs. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interpreter+argument pairs published by derp.ca (luajit.exe/vm_s390x.exe/init.exe + tcp.log/lib_bit.txt/icon.txt) — the combination of a Lua runtime executing a text-extension file is not seen in benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fakegit-campaign-uses-7600-github.html • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/
ATT&CKT1059 T1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate game mods or apps that ship an embedded luajit.exe reading a real .log config
  • Developers running Lua/LuaJIT interactively against a local tcp.log test fixture
  • Security tooling that bundles gcc.exe/init.exe for build tasks referencing .txt inputs
  • Renamed portable Lua distributions used in QA automation
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent chain — confirm the launcher is a Launch*.bat/.cmd and the interpreter sits in a user-writable dir (Downloads/Temp/extracted ZIP), not Program Files; hash the .txt payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the LuaJIT process tree, and rotate all credentials/tokens accessible from that user (StealC is the endgame). 3) Hunt: search the same host for the two persistence scheduled tasks and any outbound to polygon.drpc.org or the C2 IPs; sweep the org for the same interpreter+data-file pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("luajit.exe","lua.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","gcc.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tcp.log","uix.txt","lib_bit.txt","icon.txt","rsp.json","ptd.txt")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LaunchTool.cmd","LaunchApp.bat","Launch.bat","Launcher.cmd"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("luajit.exe","lua.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","gcc.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("tcp.log","uix.txt","lib_bit.txt","icon.txt","rsp.json","ptd.txt")
   or (ActingProcessName has "cmd.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LaunchTool.cmd","LaunchApp.bat","Launch.bat","Launcher.cmd"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SmartLoader LuaJIT Interpreter Executing Obfuscated Text-Disguised Payload
id: 6f1a9c2e-7b44-4d21-9e0a-2f5c1d8b3a41
description: Detects the FakeGit SmartLoader loader pattern where a LuaJIT interpreter (frequently renamed) is invoked with an obfuscated Lua payload disguised as a .txt/.log/.json file.
references:
  - https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fakegit-campaign-uses-7600-github.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22
tags:
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\luajit.exe'
      - '\lua.exe'
      - '\vm_s390x.exe'
      - '\init.exe'
      - '\luad.exe'
      - '\gcc.exe'
  selection_arg:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'tcp.log'
      - 'uix.txt'
      - 'lib_bit.txt'
      - 'icon.txt'
      - 'rsp.json'
      - 'ptd.txt'
  condition: selection_img and selection_arg
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\luajit.exe OR *\LuaJIT.exe OR *\vm_s390x.exe OR *\init.exe OR *\luad.exe OR *\lua.exe OR *\gcc.exe) @CommandLine:(*tcp.log* OR *uix.txt* OR *lib_bit.txt* OR *icon.txt* OR *rsp.json* OR *ptd.txt*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(luajit|lua|vm_s390x|init|luad|gcc)\.exe$/i | regex("(tcp\.log|uix\.txt|lib_bit\.txt|icon\.txt|rsp\.json|ptd\.txt)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("luajit.exe","lua.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","gcc.exe")) AND (Processes.process IN ("*tcp.log*","*uix.txt*","*lib_bit.txt*","*icon.txt*","*rsp.json*","*ptd.txt*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

SmartLoader persistence: scheduled task running a LuaJIT stage or FakeGit task names AIInstallation High
Detects the two daily scheduled tasks SmartLoader creates (names like AudioManager_ODM3 / OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757) — one runs a cached Lua stage, the other re-downloads a fresh encrypted stage from GitHub. Keys on schtasks creations whose action references the campaign's interpreters/payload files or the specific task-name tokens. Rationale: The two named tasks (AudioManager_ODM3, OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757) and a task action invoking the LuaJIT interpreter/payload are documented by derp.ca; requiring the action reference the payload avoids FP on the real OfficeClickToRunTask. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/109-fake-github-repositories-used/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Microsoft OfficeClickToRunTask maintenance (excluded because we require the campaign suffix or a Lua payload in the action)
  • Admins scripting scheduled tasks that legitimately run a bundled lua.exe
  • Software installers creating audio-manager helper tasks with unrelated actions
  • RMM tooling creating daily re-download tasks pointing at internal update servers
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (/tr) and confirm it launches a LuaJIT interpreter against a .txt/.log stage or re-downloads from GitHub; check task author and creation time. 2) Contain: delete both scheduled tasks (schtasks /delete), isolate host, kill running Lua process, and remove the cached stage files. 3) Hunt: look for the loader execution UC on the same host, outbound to polygon.drpc.org / C2 IPs, and query fleet-wide for either task name to find other victims.

SmartLoader Polygon smart-contract C2 resolution / hardcoded C2 IP callback AICommand & Control Medium
Detects SmartLoader resolving its live C2 via the Polygon blockchain dead-drop (eth_call to polygon.drpc.org against the campaign contract addresses) or beaconing to the resolved C2 IPs 89.169.12.173 / 89.169.12.241. This blockchain-dead-drop resolver is the campaign's most distinctive C2 tradecraft. Rationale: polygon.drpc.org used as an eth_call dead-drop resolver plus the two resolved C2 IPs (89.169.12.173/.241) are corroborated by derp.ca and PlanetJon; blockchain-RPC egress from an endpoint is inherently rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://www.planetjon.net/news/cybersecurity/smartloader-stealc-campaign-blockchain-c2-and-fraudulent-github-repositories/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain developers / web3 wallets on dev workstations querying polygon.drpc.org RPC
  • Crypto-trading or DeFi desktop apps that use dRPC endpoints
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a monitored VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving campaign IOCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a LuaJIT interpreter or unsigned binary hitting polygon.drpc.org/eth_call is malicious; a browser/wallet is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 89.169.12.173/.241 and the resolver at the proxy/firewall, kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the loader-execution and scheduled-task UCs on the host, pull any subsequent StealC exfil connections, and rotate every secret on the machine per Island's guidance.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("89.169.12.173","89.169.12.241") or RemoteUrl has "polygon.drpc.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("89.169.12.173","89.169.12.241") or Url has "polygon.drpc.org" or DstHostname has "polygon.drpc.org"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DnsQuery has "polygon.drpc.org"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StealC exfiltration to hardcoded FakeGit gate IPs / PHP endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the final-stage StealC infostealer POSTing collected credentials to the campaign's hardcoded gate servers 217.119.129.110 / 213.176.72.200 on the fixed path /3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php. Confirms successful compromise and active data theft. Rationale: The gate IPs 217.119.129.110 / 213.176.72.200 and the fixed StealC PHP path /3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php are documented IOCs from derp.ca; any host reaching them indicates active credential exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1555
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platforms or sandboxes actively probing the gate IPs for enrichment
  • IR responders replaying the sample in an isolated network
  • Blocklist-validation scanners confirming the endpoints are down
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the gate server is later repurposed (low, given fixed PHP path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process and whether an outbound POST occurred; a hit here is a confirmed StealC infection, not a maybe. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block both gate IPs, and treat all credentials/cookies/tokens on that endpoint as compromised — force rotation and revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: back-trace to the loader and scheduled-task UCs, identify what browsers/apps StealC harvested, and sweep IdP sign-in logs for anomalous use of the stolen sessions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200") or RemoteUrl has "3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200") or Url has "3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpRequestMethod=HttpMethod),
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200")
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeGit GitHub dead-drop stage download by LuaJIT/LOLBin process AIDelivery Medium
Detects SmartLoader pulling encrypted follow-on stages from the campaign's GitHub dead-drop repositories (rd898/package, Mahmudul-Riad/www) when the requesting process is a LuaJIT interpreter or download LOLBin rather than a browser. Catches the mid-chain staging that survives repo takedowns. Rationale: The dead-drop repo paths (rd898/package json/1.json, Mahmudul-Riad/www index/7.txt) from derp.ca are specific; gating on a Lua interpreter or LOLBin as the requester (not a browser) removes benign GitHub browsing noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/109-fake-github-repositories-used/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately cloning/curling one of the named GitHub accounts before takedown
  • CI pipelines mirroring GitHub raw content via curl/powershell to unrelated repos of similar name
  • Security researchers downloading the stage files for analysis
  • GitHub raw path collisions if the account names are reused after suspension
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process pulling the stage is a Lua interpreter or scripted LOLBin, and capture the downloaded blob (hex/XOR/base64url/AES-ECB chained). 2) Contain: isolate host, block the GitHub raw paths at the proxy, and kill the loader process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Polygon C2 and StealC exfil UCs on the same host; report the still-live GitHub accounts to GitHub abuse and sweep the org for other hosts touching these repos.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("rd898/package","Mahmudul-Riad/www","/json/1.json","/json/2.json","/index/7.txt","/index/8.txt")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("luajit.exe","lua.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","gcc.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("rd898/package","Mahmudul-Riad/www","/json/1.json","/json/2.json","/index/7.txt","/index/8.txt")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or SHA1 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or MD5 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or SHA1 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or MD5 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea PR-update endpoint abuse — POST to /api/v1/repos/*/pulls/*/update (CVE-2026-58443) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to the Gitea pull-request update route that CVE-2026-58443 abuses, where a public-only,write:repository token has its scope checked against the public base repo but pushes into a private head branch. Surfaces every invocation of the vulnerable endpoint for repo-boundary review, since the public-route/private-target mismatch manifests at the web tier only as a call to this exact path. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory (POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update) as a regex against web/proxy access logs; the regex-anchored numeric PR index and repos path segment make it far tighter than a generic /update match. Cross-checked GitLab advisory DB and Gitea 1.27.0 release notes. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.27.0/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1068 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Repo maintainer clicking 'Update branch' on a legitimate PR (fires the same endpoint)
  • CI/CD or bot service account keeping fork PR branches in sync with base
  • Automated merge-queue tooling that rebases/updates PR heads before merge
  • GUI-driven updates proxied through the same route (indistinguishable from API/token calls at the web tier)
  • Load-balancer/health-probe replays of a captured request in test environments
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Gitea-Actions" and SourceUserName !endswith "-ci" and SourceUserName !endswith "-bot"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request context for each hit — SourceUserName/token, SourceIP, User-Agent, and the base owner/repo/PR index. In Gitea admin, resolve the PR: is the HEAD repository private while the base repo is public? If yes, and the caller's token is public-only scoped, treat as exploitation. 2) Contain: revoke the offending personal access token, block the source IP at the WAF, and confirm Gitea is upgraded to >=1.27.0 (fix for CVE-2026-58443); if still on <=1.26.4, prioritize patch. 3) Hunt: review the private head repo's branch history for unexpected merge commits ('Merge branch ... into ...') and any Actions workflow runs triggered by the pushed update; enumerate all public-only tokens and their recent API activity against private resources.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update"
| extend BaseOwner = extract(@"(?i)/api/v1/repos/([^/]+)/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update", 1, RequestURL)
| extend BaseRepo  = extract(@"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/([^/]+)/pulls/[0-9]+/update", 1, RequestURL)
| extend PrIndex   = extract(@"(?i)/pulls/([0-9]+)/update", 1, RequestURL)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestClientApplication, DestinationHostName, BaseOwner, BaseRepo, PrIndex, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gitea Public-Only Token PR Update Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-58443)
id: 6b0f2e94-2c1a-4d77-9a3e-8f1c4b7d2a55
description: Detects HTTP POST to the Gitea pull-request update route abused by CVE-2026-58443, where a public-only,write:repository token can push public base commits into a private PR head branch. Endpoint access is the web-tier signature of the public-route/private-target authorization mismatch.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxjv-752h-3vp2
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22
tags:
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1550.001
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: 'POST'
    cs-uri-stem|re: '/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate PR head-branch updates by repo authors, maintainers or CI/CD service accounts
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*/api/v1/repos/*/pulls/*/update*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.user, Web.http_user_agent, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=url "/api/v1/repos/(?<base_owner>[^/]+)/(?<base_repo>[^/]+)/pulls/(?<pr_index>\d+)/update"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime lastTime src dest user http_user_agent base_owner base_repo pr_index url count
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*/api/v1/repos/*/pulls/*/update*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.user, Web.http_user_agent, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rex field=url "/api/v1/repos/(?<base_owner>[^/]+)/(?<base_repo>[^/]+)/pulls/(?<pr_index>\d+)/update"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime lastTime src dest user http_user_agent base_owner base_repo pr_index url count
| sort - lastTime
Anomalous / first-seen actor calling Gitea PR-update route (CVE-2026-58443 exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Baselines which accounts/tokens normally invoke the Gitea pull-request update endpoint per environment (typically PR authors, maintainers and CI service accounts) and flags callers with no prior history hitting it. CVE-2026-58443 abuse originates from an under-privileged public-only token that would not normally update PR head branches, so a first-seen caller of this route is a high-value outlier. Rationale: Anti-joins the set of accounts that legitimately updated a PR in the trailing 30 days against today's callers of the exact CVE-2026-58443 route, isolating first-seen actors (the profile of an attacker wielding an under-scoped public-only token). Route regex is anchored to the advisory's endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.27.0/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A new maintainer or contributor legitimately updating a PR for the first time
  • Newly onboarded CI/CD service account whose token first appears this window
  • Rotated/renamed token that presents as a new SourceUserName despite same human owner
  • Migration or bulk-sync job that touches many PRs on its first run
  • Analyst or admin manually testing the patched endpoint after upgrade
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !endswith "-ci" and SourceUserName !endswith "-bot" and RequestClientApplication !has "GiteaActions"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each first-seen caller, identify the token scope in Gitea admin (Settings > Applications / token audit). A public-only,write:repository token hitting this route against a PR whose HEAD repo is private is the exploitation signature. 2) Contain: revoke the token, block the SourceIP at the WAF, and verify the Gitea instance is >=1.27.0; snapshot the affected private repo before further changes. 3) Hunt: expand to all routes the same token touched in the last 30d, check for CVE-2026-58444 (private-content disclosure via GET /{owner}/{repo}) from the same principal, and review private head branches for injected merge commits and downstream Actions runs.
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 1d;
let routeRegex = @"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update";
let baselineCallers = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
    | where RequestMethod == "POST" and RequestURL matches regex routeRegex
    | summarize by SourceUserName;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where RequestMethod == "POST" and RequestURL matches regex routeRegex
| join kind=leftanti baselineCallers on SourceUserName   // callers never seen updating a PR in the prior 30d
| summarize Hits = count(), SrcIPs = make_set(SourceIP, 20), Routes = make_set(RequestURL, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceUserName, RequestClientApplication
| order by Hits desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="POST" Web.url="*/api/v1/repos/*/pulls/*/update*" earliest=-30d by Web.user, Web.src, Web.url, _time span=1d
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eventstats min(_time) as first_seen_epoch by user

Gitea Actions artifact signed-URL HMAC reuse across differing task/artifact tuples (CVE-2026-58426) AIExploitation High
Hunts the defining signal of CVE-2026-58426: a single Gitea Actions V4 artifact signature (sig=) presented alongside two or more distinct (taskID, artifactName) query tuples. Because the HMAC is built from delimiter-less concatenated fields, an attacker rewrites taskID/artifactName/artifactID while preserving the signature to read or write another task's artifacts. A legitimate signed URL is bound to exactly one tuple, so signature reuse across tuples is high-fidelity exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint names (DownloadArtifact/UploadArtifact) and the concrete signed-URL params sig/taskID/artifactName from routers/api/actions/artifactsv4.go. The dcount(tuple)>1-per-signature keys directly on the root cause (delimiter-less HMAC input) and is near-impossible to trigger legitimately since Gitea issues one signature per fixed tuple. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/gitea-actions-artifacts-hmac-ambiguity-allows-cross-repository-access/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI runner retries a transient upload/download using a cached signed URL (same sig, same tuple — excluded by DistinctTuples>1)
  • Load balancer/proxy log duplication replays identical URLs (same tuple, filtered out)
  • Automated artifact-integrity scanners that re-request the same signed URL verbatim
  • URL-rewriting proxies that append tracking params but leave sig/taskID/artifactName intact (still same tuple)
Suppression filter
| where DistinctTuples > 1 and array_length(SrcIps) >= 1  // require real tuple divergence; extend with `| where SrcIps !has "<known-ci-egress-ip>"` per environment if a retrying runner is confirmed benign
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged Sig, list the distinct (taskID, artifactName) tuples and source IPs; confirm whether the tuples belong to different runs/repositories — cross-repo tuples on one signature is confirmed exploitation. 2) CONTAIN: Rotate GetGeneralTokenSigningSecret and upgrade Gitea to >=1.26.2 (patched); temporarily disable Actions artifact V4 endpoints at the proxy if patching is delayed. 3) HUNT: For the offending source IP/runner, enumerate all UploadArtifact PUTs (integrity risk to victim tasks) and DownloadArtifact GETs against private-repo runs; review FinalizeArtifact activity for tampered artifacts and audit which private repos had running tasks during the window.
// Gitea artifact signed-URL HMAC reuse (CVE-2026-58426). Point at the reverse-proxy/WAF logs fronting Gitea.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has_any ("DownloadArtifact","UploadArtifact")
| extend Sig = extract(@"(?i)[?&]sig=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend TaskID = extract(@"(?i)[?&]taskID=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend ArtifactName = extract(@"(?i)[?&]artifactName=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(Sig)
| extend Tuple = strcat(TaskID, "|", ArtifactName)
| summarize DistinctTuples = dcount(Tuple),
            Tuples = make_set(Tuple, 50),
            SrcIps = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20),
            Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 5),
            Requests = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by Sig
| where DistinctTuples > 1   // one signature, >1 tuple = HMAC-boundary collision abuse
| order by DistinctTuples desc

Gitea single source reads artifacts across many task/repository contexts in short window (CVE-2026-58426 cross-repo read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the DownloadArtifact exploit path of CVE-2026-58426: one client rewriting signed URLs to pull artifacts from many unrelated task/run contexts, escaping its own repository scope. Detects a single source IP issuing DownloadArtifact GETs spanning 3+ distinct taskID/artifactName tuples within a tight window — the fan-out shape of cross-repository private-artifact disclosure. Rationale: Grounded in the article's DownloadArtifact path (cross-task/cross-repo read, C:H) and its exact URL params. A benign CI job downloads only the artifacts of its own run; 3+ distinct task contexts from one source in a short window matches the described URL-rewrite scope escape. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1213 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate matrix/monorepo job that legitimately downloads many artifacts from its own run within one window
  • An artifact-mirroring or backup job that bulk-pulls artifacts across projects with proper authorization
  • A shared CI egress NAT where several distinct runners appear as one SrcIpAddr
  • A dependency-caching workflow that fans out downloads across upstream build tasks
Suppression filter
| where DistinctContexts >= 3 and Downloads < 500  // suppress high-volume authorized mirror/backup jobs; tune per environment and allowlist known runner egress IPs via `| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<ci-nat-ip>")`
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the distinct taskIDs belong to different runs/repositories than the source runner's own job; same-run downloads are benign. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the proxy and suspend the associated runner/user token; upgrade Gitea to >=1.26.2. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the enumerated taskIDs to identify which private repositories were exposed, check whether those artifacts contained secrets/tokens, and review UploadArtifact activity from the same source for a paired write primitive.
// Gitea cross-context artifact download fan-out (CVE-2026-58426). Point at the proxy/WAF logs fronting Gitea.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "DownloadArtifact"
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| extend TaskID = extract(@"(?i)[?&]taskID=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend ArtifactName = extract(@"(?i)[?&]artifactName=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend Ctx = strcat(TaskID, "|", ArtifactName)
| summarize DistinctContexts = dcount(Ctx),
            Contexts = make_set(Ctx, 50),
            Downloads = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctContexts >= 3   // one source pulling >=3 distinct task/artifact contexts in 5 min = cross-repo scraping
| order by DistinctContexts desc

Gitea UploadArtifact PUT writes reused across foreign task contexts (CVE-2026-58426 cross-task write) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the UploadArtifact integrity path of CVE-2026-58426: a signed upload URL rewritten to append attacker data into another task's artifact staging context and mutate its metadata (I:H). Detects UploadArtifact PUT requests where one signature or one source is used against 2+ distinct task/artifact tuples — the write-side of the HMAC-boundary collision that FinalizeArtifact later consumes. Rationale: Uses the article's UploadArtifact PUT path (appendUploadChunkV3 + UpdateArtifactByID metadata mutation, I:H) and the concrete sig/taskID/artifactName params. Scoping to write methods plus signature-tuple divergence isolates the integrity-tampering primitive from normal single-tuple uploads. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1565.002 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A chunked upload where the client legitimately re-PUTs the same tuple across retries (same tuple — excluded by DistinctTuples>1)
  • Resumable upload libraries that split one artifact into multiple PUTs but keep taskID/artifactName constant
  • Proxy retransmission of a failed PUT with an identical URL
  • A runner uploading several distinctly-named artifacts of its OWN task (different artifactName, same taskID — inspect whether taskID also diverges before escalating)
Suppression filter
| where DistinctTuples > 1 and array_length(set_intersect(Tuples, Tuples)) > 0  // core signal is tuple divergence per signature; if resumable-upload retries cause noise, additionally require dcount over the taskID portion only
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the flagged signature's tuples reference different taskIDs (not just different artifactNames within one task); differing taskIDs on one upload signature is confirmed cross-task write. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the affected artifacts' storage staging path, block the source, and upgrade to >=1.26.2; hold FinalizeArtifact processing for the impacted runs. 3) HUNT: Verify integrity of any artifact whose taskID appears as a write target (compare FileSize/FileCompressedSize against expected), rotate GetGeneralTokenSigningSecret, and check downstream consumers/deployments that ingested the tampered artifacts.
// Gitea cross-task artifact upload-state write (CVE-2026-58426). Point at the proxy/WAF logs fronting Gitea.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "UploadArtifact"
| where HttpMethod in~ ("PUT","POST")
| extend Sig = extract(@"(?i)[?&]sig=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend TaskID = extract(@"(?i)[?&]taskID=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| extend ArtifactName = extract(@"(?i)[?&]artifactName=([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(Sig)
| extend Tuple = strcat(TaskID, "|", ArtifactName)
| summarize DistinctTuples = dcount(Tuple),
            Tuples = make_set(Tuple, 50),
            SrcIps = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20),
            Writes = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by Sig
| where DistinctTuples > 1   // one upload signature spanning >1 task/artifact tuple = cross-task staging write
| order by Writes desc

Inbound X-WEBAUTH-USER header at edge/WAF from non-loopback source (Gitea CVE-2026-20896) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests carrying an X-WEBAUTH-USER header that arrive at the reverse proxy / WAF from a source IP outside the trusted-proxy range (anything other than loopback). Because the Gitea Docker image ships REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * with ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION, any client that can inject this header is authenticated as the named user with no password or cookie. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact attack primitive — the X-WEBAUTH-USER header string arriving from a non-loopback source IP — which is only ever legitimate from the co-located proxy (127.0.0.0/8 / ::1). Any external source IP asserting this header is the CVE-2026-20896 impersonation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The authenticating reverse proxy itself is deployed on a separate host with a routable IP (not loopback) and legitimately injects the header — tune SourceIP to that proxy's address
  • Security scanners / DAST tools replaying headers during authorized testing
  • A load balancer / service mesh sidecar in the request path that forwards the header on behalf of the proxy
  • Internal health-check probes that spoof identity headers for monitoring
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP != "<your-reverse-proxy-ip>"  // remove this line and instead allowlist the real proxy address if it is non-loopback
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is NOT the configured reverse proxy — check the offending request's asserted username (extract from Message) and whether it targets admin/gitea_admin. 2) Contain: set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's real IP (or 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128) and upgrade gitea to >=1.26.3; block direct network access to the Gitea container port so only the proxy can reach it. 3) Hunt: pivot on that SourceIP and asserted username across Gitea audit logs for repo clones, token/SSH key creation, and admin actions performed while impersonated.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER" or RequestContext has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and SourceIP != "::1"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Message, RequestContext
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Inbound X-WEBAUTH-USER header from non-loopback source (Gitea CVE-2026-20896)
id: 9f2c1a44-7e6b-4d21-b0f2-1c8a4e2b91aa
description: Detects HTTP requests bearing an X-WEBAUTH-USER header from a source IP that is not the trusted loopback proxy, indicating direct identity injection against a Gitea instance with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = *.

  filter_loopback:

      - '::1'

level: high
APPLICATION
search index=proxy OR index=web ("X-WEBAUTH-USER") NOT (src="127.0.0.1" OR src="::1") | rex field=_raw "(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*(?<webauth_user>[^\s,;]+)" | where isnotnull(webauth_user) | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(webauth_user) as asserted_users by src dest | sort - count
Same Gitea X-WEBAUTH-USER identity asserted from multiple distinct source IPs AIExploitation Medium
Correlation hunt: a single X-WEBAUTH-USER identity value asserted from two or more distinct source IPs within a short window. Under normal reverse-proxy auth a given user's identity is only ever injected by the one trusted proxy; multiple source IPs for the same asserted user indicates direct header spoofing exploiting CVE-2026-20896. Rationale: Legitimate reverse-proxy auth injects each user's identity from exactly one proxy IP; the fan-out of a single asserted username across multiple source IPs is a high-fidelity signal of the header-injection impersonation described in the advisory, and needs no known bad IP to fire.
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A highly-available proxy tier (multiple proxy nodes) all legitimately inject the header from their own IPs — allowlist the proxy pool
  • NAT / egress IP rotation in front of a single genuine proxy
  • Blue-team validation replaying the PoC from several test hosts
  • CDN edge nodes forwarding the header from multiple PoPs
Suppression filter
| where DistinctSourceIPs >= 2 and not (SourceIPs has_any ("<proxy-node-1-ip>", "<proxy-node-2-ip>"))  // keep the >=2 logic but drop legit multi-node proxy pools by allowlisting their IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: review SourceIPs set for the flagged WebAuthUser — legitimate output is a single proxy IP; multiple public IPs asserting 'admin' or 'gitea_admin' is critical. 2) Contain: restrict REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy IP(s), patch to gitea >=1.26.3, and firewall the container port to the proxy only. 3) Hunt: for each spoofed identity, review Gitea actions (new access tokens, deploy keys, webhook creation, repo mirroring) taken from the untrusted source IPs and rotate any credentials that account could reach.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| extend WebAuthUser = extract(@"(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*([^\s,;]+)", 1, Message)
| where isnotempty(WebAuthUser)
| where not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and SourceIP != "::1"
| summarize DistinctSourceIPs = dcount(SourceIP), SourceIPs = make_set(SourceIP, 20), Requests = count() by WebAuthUser, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctSourceIPs >= 2   // one identity asserted from >=2 IPs in an hour = spoofing, not a single proxy
| order by DistinctSourceIPs desc
APPLICATION
search index=proxy OR index=web ("X-WEBAUTH-USER") | rex field=_raw "(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*(?<webauth_user>[^\s,;]+)" | where isnotnull(webauth_user) AND NOT (src="127.0.0.1" OR src="::1") | stats dc(src) as distinct_src values(src) as src_ips count as requests by webauth_user | where distinct_src>=2 | sort - distinct_src
Enumeration of Gitea app.ini config exposing REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects HTTP requests that attempt to read or enumerate the Gitea configuration file (app.ini / custom/conf/app.ini) returning a successful response. Attackers probe for the file to confirm the vulnerable REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * default before exploiting CVE-2026-20896. Rationale: Uses the article's named configuration paths (custom/conf/app.ini) and the REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES setting they contain; a 200 on these paths is a strong pre-exploitation recon indicator specific to this Gitea misconfiguration.
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin fetching app.ini through an authenticated admin panel
  • Config-management / backup tooling pulling the file over HTTP
  • Vulnerability scanners in an authorized assessment window

1) Triage: confirm the request path resolved to the real Gitea config (200 with config content) and identify the SourceIP; check whether the same IP subsequently sent X-WEBAUTH-USER headers. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, ensure the config file is not web-servable, and patch/reconfigure trusted proxies. 3) Hunt: search for follow-on X-WEBAUTH-USER injection (UC1/UC2) from the same source and review any repo access that followed.
