wp2shell webshell interaction: HTTP requests to executable PHP under /wp-content/cache/ AICommand & Control High
Hunts inbound requests to any .php file located under /wp-content/cache/ — post-exploitation interaction with the planted wp2shell backdoor. SANS ISC noted the shell returns a fake 404, so status code is unreliable; the path itself is the signal because WordPress never serves PHP from its cache directory. Rationale: Directly from the SANS ISC report (webshell created under /cache/ returning a fake 404); requesting an executable PHP from the cache directory is an unambiguous backdoor-interaction signal that is status-code independent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/18/wordpress-vulnerabilities-wp2shell-cve-2026-60137-cve-2026-60137/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Caching plugins that legitimately serve a .php cache handler from wp-content/cache (rare legacy WP Super Cache setups)
  • Security scanners fuzzing common webshell paths under wp-content
  • Uptime/monitoring probes configured against a specific cache path
  • A developer's leftover debug PHP endpoint in the cache dir
Suppression filter
| where Url !has "/cache/wp-rocket/" and Url !has "/cache/supercache/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the requested cache-path .php with a matching file-write event (UC2). If the file exists on disk and analysts didn't create it, treat as confirmed webshell. Inspect POST bodies/params for command strings. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr, delete the file, and rotate wp-config keys + DB creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate every SrcIpAddr that touched the path, review commands executed, and check for lateral movement, new admin users, and outbound connections from the web host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/wp-content/cache/[^?\s]*\.php"
| summarize Hits=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,10), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,5), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by Hits desc

wp2shell LFI: wp-config credential theft via admin-ajax.php AIExploitation Medium
Hunts local file inclusion attempts against wp-config through admin-ajax.php — a wp2shell post-exploitation step Wiz observed to retrieve WordPress database credentials and authentication keys. Flags admin-ajax.php requests carrying wp-config references, path traversal, or php://filter wrappers. Rationale: Based on Wiz's observed activity: 'Local file inclusion attempts targeting wp-config through admin-ajax.php to retrieve database credentials and authentication keys' — admin-ajax.php combined with wp-config/traversal/php-filter markers is a precise LFI signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Plugins that legitimately pass file paths through admin-ajax.php actions (some backup/migration plugins)
  • Security scanners testing LFI payloads against admin-ajax.php
  • URL-encoded query values containing '../' as benign relative references
  • Analyst/pentest validation of the disclosed chain against owned assets
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the admin-ajax.php request actually references wp-config and check the response size/status — a large 200 suggests the file was disclosed. 2) Contain: block the source IP, and because wp-config keys/salts and DB creds may be exposed, immediately rotate all WordPress secret keys/salts and reset the database password. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP later authenticated to wp-admin, created admin users, or dropped a webshell (UC2/UC3), and review DB access logs for the exposed credentials.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "admin-ajax.php"
| where Url has_any ("wp-config", "php://filter", "../", "..%2f", "..%252f")
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by Requests desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

AWS Kiro Flaw Let a Poisoned Web Page Rewrite Its Config and Run Code

The Hacker News
2026-07-21 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Hidden text on a web page was enough to make Kiro, AWS's agentic coding IDE, rewrite its own configuration file and run an attacker's code on a developer's machine, with no approval step able to stop it. Intezer, in research with Kodem Security, found that a request as ordinary as asking Kiro to summarize a page could end in remote code execution. AWS has patched the issue, and no CVE has been

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kiro process spawning shell / interpreter child (rogue MCP server start command) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Kiro (AWS agentic IDE) writing protected config files mcp.json / .vscode tasks.json · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kiro-spawned interpreter beaconing to external host (rogue MCP server C2)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Kiro (AWS agentic IDE) writing protected config files mcp.json / .vscode tasks.json AIInstallation High
Hunts the core primitive of the Intezer/Kodem Kiro chain: the Kiro process itself writing ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json (which registers MCP-server start commands that auto-execute on reload) or .vscode/tasks.json / settings.json (CVE-2026-10591 auto-exec on folder open). A poisoned web page fetched by Kiro drives fsWrite to these files with no effective approval, turning a config edit into code execution. Rationale: Uses the exact article artifacts: the Kiro process (fsWrite) writing ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json and the .vscode/tasks.json|settings.json auto-exec files named in the Intezer, Rehberger (Embrace The Red) and Cymulate (CVE-2026-10591) findings. Constraining the writer to a Kiro process on these specific paths is the highest-fidelity form of the primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-10591 • https://embracethered.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1059 T1554 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adding/editing an MCP server through the Kiro UI, which writes mcp.json normally
  • Format-on-save or workspace-trust changes rewriting .vscode/settings.json
  • Kiro adding a build/lint task to .vscode/tasks.json at user request
  • Extension or Kiro version update rewriting workspace config
  • Team member syncing a shared .vscode config committed to the repo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bash","sh -c","python","curl","wget","nc ","osascript","base64") or FileName == "mcp.json"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the written mcp.json/tasks.json content (or nearest DeviceFileEvents delta) — inspect any newly added MCP server 'command'/'args' or task shell command for interpreters, curl/wget, or base64. Confirm whether the user was actively fetching/summarising an external URL at that time. 2) Contain: if the config references an unexpected binary or network callback, isolate the host, kill the spawned server process, and revert mcp.json/.vscode files; verify Kiro is on >=1.0.x (protected-paths fix). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for a Kiro-child interpreter and outbound beacon (UC2/UC3), and search other developer endpoints for the same injected server 'command' string.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "/.kiro/settings" and FileName =~ "mcp.json")
     or (FolderPath has "/.vscode" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","settings.json"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "kiro"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has "/.kiro/settings" and TargetFileName =~ "mcp.json")
     or (TargetFilePath has "/.vscode" and TargetFileName in~ ("tasks.json","settings.json"))
| where ActingProcessName has "kiro"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kiro Agentic IDE Writing Protected Config Files (mcp.json / .vscode)
id: 3a1f2c5e-7b64-4d9a-9f21-8c0e5b1a4d77
description: Detects the Kiro AWS agentic coding IDE writing its MCP server config or VS Code task/settings files, the write-to-execute primitive abused by the Intezer/Kodem prompt-injection chain and CVE-2026-10591.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.t1554
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_kiro_mcp:
    ActingProcessName|contains: 'kiro'
    TargetFilePath|contains: '/.kiro/settings'
    TargetFileName: 'mcp.json'
  selection_vscode:
    ActingProcessName|contains: 'kiro'
    TargetFilePath|contains: '/.vscode'
    TargetFileName:
      - 'tasks.json'
      - 'settings.json'
  condition: selection_kiro_mcp or selection_vscode
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| (TargetFileName=/\/\.kiro\/settings\/mcp\.json$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/\.vscode\/(tasks|settings)\.json$/i)
| ContextImageFileName=/kiro/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="mcp.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.kiro/settings/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="tasks.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="settings.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="mcp.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.kiro/settings/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="tasks.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="settings.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Kiro process spawning shell / interpreter child (rogue MCP server start command) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution of the injected MCP server: after Kiro reloads a poisoned mcp.json it launches the server's start command on the host with the developer's privileges. Surfaces Kiro as the parent of a shell or scripting interpreter (bash/sh/zsh/python/node/osascript/curl), which is how the attacker's arbitrary command runs. Rationale: Directly targets the article's execution step — Kiro launching the MCP server's start command as a host process with developer privileges. Kiro-as-parent of a raw shell/scripting interpreter (esp. osascript/curl/nc) is the anomaly; kept hunting-tier because Kiro legitimately spawns node/python for real MCP servers and its integrated terminal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://www.intezer.com/ • https://embracethered.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP servers Kiro launches as node/python child processes
  • Developer using Kiro's integrated terminal to run bash/zsh/python
  • Kiro build/test tasks invoking shell commands
  • Language servers or linters spawned by the IDE
  • Git or package-manager hooks (curl/wget) triggered from the IDE terminal
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","base64","curl","wget","/tmp/","bash -i","osascript","IEX","Invoke-Expression") or FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","osascript")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessCommandLine of the child — legitimate MCP servers run known package paths; flag inline shell one-liners, base64, curl|bash, osascript, or reverse-shell tooling. Correlate the child's start time against a preceding mcp.json/tasks.json write (UC1) within seconds. 2) Contain: kill the child process tree, isolate the host if the command is clearly malicious, and revert Kiro config files. 3) Hunt: check the child process for outbound beaconing (UC3) and enumerate other dev hosts running the same command string or contacting the same destination.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "kiro"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","python","python3","node","osascript","curl","wget","nc","ncat","pwsh","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "kiro"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","/sh","zsh","python","node","osascript","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","pwsh","powershell")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kiro Agentic IDE Spawning Shell or Interpreter Child
id: b7d4e0a2-1c93-4f6b-8a55-2e9f7c3d6b41
description: Detects the Kiro AWS agentic IDE spawning a shell or scripting interpreter, consistent with execution of a rogue MCP server start command written into mcp.json via prompt injection.
references:

Kiro-spawned interpreter beaconing to external host (rogue MCP server C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 behaviour proven in Intezer's PoC: the rogue MCP server (a child of Kiro) phones home on a fixed short interval (every ~10 seconds in the demo) exfiltrating hostname, username and platform. Surfaces high-count, regular outbound connections from Kiro-child interpreter processes to an external destination. Rationale: Encodes the PoC's fixed ~10-second beacon of host/user/platform and ties the network activity to a Kiro-child interpreter (Defender via InitiatingProcessParentFileName; Sentinel via an ImProcessCreate->ImNetworkSession host+time join since ImNetworkSession carries no process attribution). Threshold-based, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://www.intezer.com/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP servers (node/python) making frequent API calls to a remote endpoint
  • Kiro AI backend/telemetry connections polling a cloud service
  • Package managers (npm/pip) pulling dependencies via node/python
  • Developer scripts run from the IDE terminal polling an internal API
  • Language-model or linter processes streaming to a SaaS endpoint
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and Ports != dynamic([443])
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RemoteIP/destination and the child process command line — whitelisted SaaS/MCP endpoints are benign; a raw IP, dynamic-DNS, or localhost-in-testing pattern plus fixed short intervals is suspicious. Confirm the connecting process descends from Kiro and correlate with a recent mcp.json write (UC1) and interpreter spawn (UC2). 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, kill the beaconing process, and revert Kiro config. 3) Hunt: sweep other developer endpoints for the same destination IP/domain and identical mcp.json server 'command' string; assess whether credentials or source code left the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "kiro"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), IntervalBuckets = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 10s)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 8)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 30    // ~10s beacon sustained over several minutes
| order by ConnCount desc
let KiroChildren = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has "kiro"
    | project DvcHostname, ChildStart = TimeGenerated, ChildProcess = ActingProcessName;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection))
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| join kind=inner KiroChildren on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ChildStart .. ChildStart + 1h)
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ChildProcess, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount >= 30    // ~10s beacon sustained over several minutes
| order by ConnCount desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|python3?|bash|osascript|curl|wget|nc|ncat)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 30

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Critical SharePoint RCE CVE-2026-50522 Under Active Exploitation After Public PoC

The Hacker News
2026-07-21 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A third SharePoint Server flaw patched by Microsoft as part of its Patch Tuesday update for July 2026 has come under active exploitation, per watchTowr. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-50522 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical deserialization of untrusted data in Microsoft Office SharePoint that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. Microsoft credited DEVCORE

CVEsCVE-2026-50522 CVE-2026-58644 CVE-2026-56164 CVE-2026-32201 CVE-2026-45659
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint machine-key theft via unauth POST to ToolPane.aspx with SignOut referer (CVE-2026-50522) · [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning shell/LOLBin (CVE-2026-50522 deserialization RCE) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ASPX webshell / machine-key exfil file written to SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (CVE-2026-50522 persistence) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
SharePoint machine-key theft via unauth POST to ToolPane.aspx with SignOut referer (CVE-2026-50522) AIExploitation High
Hunts the single unauthenticated request that pulls SharePoint IIS machine keys by POSTing a .NET deserialization payload to the sign-in/ToolPane endpoint with a forged Referer to SignOut.aspx (the ToolShell auth-bypass shape corroborated for this CVE). This is the CVE-2026-50522 exploitation primitive watchTowr and Defused Cyber observed in the wild. Rationale: Uses the article's stated primitive (unauthenticated single request to a SharePoint sign-in endpoint delivering a .NET deserialization payload to steal machine keys) grounded in the corroborated ToolShell endpoint pair ToolPane.aspx + SignOut.aspx Referer. Empty csUserName plus the SignOut referer is the auth-bypass tell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the CVE-2026-50522 check with a benign POST
  • Red-team / pentest replaying the public PoC during an authorized engagement
  • Load-balancer health checks configured to POST to _layouts endpoints (rare)
  • Legitimate SharePoint web-part editing that genuinely traverses ToolPane.aspx (will carry an authenticated csUserName and a normal same-page referer, not SignOut.aspx)
Suppression filter
| where isempty(csUserName) or csUserName == "-"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the request had empty/anonymous csUserName and a SignOut.aspx referer; pull the full csUriQuery and request body from WAF logs for __VIEWSTATE/deserialization markers. Cross-check the source cIP against threat intel. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the SharePoint server, and because machine keys may be stolen, immediately rotate ASP.NET machineKey (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey) across the farm and reset the service account per watchTowr guidance — patching alone is insufficient. 3) HUNT: Pivot to w3wp.exe child processes and new .aspx files under TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS on the same host (see companion UCs); search all farm servers for the same source IP and forged-ViewState follow-on requests.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx" or csUriStem has "/_layouts/15/signout.aspx"
| where csReferer has "/SignOut.aspx"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, csUserName, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint IIS worker w3wp.exe spawning shell/LOLBin (CVE-2026-50522 deserialization RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts post-exploitation code execution from CVE-2026-50522: the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or download LOLBins as a direct result of the .NET deserialization RCE. w3wp.exe should almost never parent an interactive shell. Rationale: w3wp.exe is the SharePoint IIS worker; the corroborating ToolShell write-ups document w3wp.exe -> cmd.exe -> powershell as the deserialization-RCE execution chain. A SharePoint worker parenting an interactive shell/LOLBin is inherently high-fidelity and article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/sharepoint-vulnerability-rce-active-exploitation-detections-mitigations • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs or provisioning scripts that legitimately shell out (rare; usually via OWSTIMER.exe not w3wp.exe)
  • Admin-authored custom web parts that invoke cmd/PowerShell by design
  • Monitoring agents injecting into w3wp for diagnostics
  • Patch/config tooling (PSConfig) running during a maintenance window — correlate with change tickets
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "OWSTIMER", "stsadm -o") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any -EncodedCommand, look for whoami/net/certutil recon or download strings; confirm the host is a SharePoint farm server. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate the SharePoint service-account credential and farm machineKey (assume key theft). 3) HUNT: Look for new .aspx files under TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS (companion UC), outbound C2 from w3wp children, and the originating ToolPane.aspx POST in IIS logs to tie back to initial access.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","net.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\net.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX webshell / machine-key exfil file written to SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (CVE-2026-50522 persistence) AIInstallation High
Hunts persistence after CVE-2026-50522 exploitation: the SharePoint worker w3wp.exe writing a new .aspx/.ashx/.asmx file (e.g. the corroborated spinstall0.aspx) into the SharePoint TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS web root to drop a webshell or dump the machine key for stealthy re-entry. Rationale: The article states persistence via machine-key theft and malware deployment; corroborating ToolShell reporting names spinstall0.aspx dropped into the LAYOUTS web root by w3wp.exe. A web-server worker writing executable .aspx into its own served directory is a textbook webshell-persistence signal, tightly scoped to SharePoint paths. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/on-prem-sharepoint-toolshell-backdoor-advisory/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patching/PSConfig or solution (WSP) deployment writing legitimate .aspx layout pages
  • SharePoint feature activation provisioning new application pages
  • Backup/restore or content-migration tooling recreating LAYOUTS files
  • Developer deploying a custom farm solution during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig", "stsadm", "Install-SPSolution"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve and read the dropped file — short files that echo web.config machineKey/ValidationKey or contain eval/Request("") webshell logic are confirmations; check the SHA256 against intel and compare creation time to any ToolPane.aspx POST. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, isolate the host, rotate the farm machineKey and SharePoint service-account credential (assume key stolen), and force-recycle app pools. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all farm servers for the same filename/hash, review IIS logs for GETs to the dropped path (webshell interaction), and check for forged __VIEWSTATE requests indicating the stolen key is already in use.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FolderPath has "\\Web Server Extensions\\" or FolderPath has "\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS\\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName =~ "spinstall0.aspx"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Qilin Ransomware Attackers Exploit PAN-OS Authentication Bypass for Initial Access

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-07-21 20 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors have been observed exploiting a now-patched high-severity Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability as an entry point to deploy Qilin (aka Agenda) ransomware on victim environments. Arctic Wolf Labs said it investigated multiple intrusions in June 2026 that began with the exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw affecting the portal and gateway

Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Inbound PAN-OS SSL VPN sessions from Qilin CVE-2026-0257 attacker IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound GlobalProtect portal/gateway activity on Palo Alto firewalls originating from the source IPs Arctic Wolf tied to CVE-2026-0257 authentication-bypass exploitation preceding Qilin ransomware. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact attacker infrastructure hitting the vulnerable PAN-OS portal/gateway components. Rationale: Uses the 20 attacker source IPs Arctic Wolf published for the CVE-2026-0257 PAN-OS auth-bypass intrusions; any of these touching a GlobalProtect portal/gateway is a direct initial-access signal.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN concentrator behind a shared cloud NAT egress that coincidentally reuses a hosting-provider IP (Vultr/DigitalOcean ranges)
  • Penetration-test or red-team engagement sourced from a rented VPS in the same block
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation service probing the portal
  • Legitimate remote worker on a datacenter/VPN-provider egress IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SourceIP established an authenticated GlobalProtect session and to which internal host/subnet; pull the associated username and check if that account normally VPNs. 2) Contain: terminate the VPN session, disable the account, and block the source IP at the firewall; verify PAN-OS is patched for CVE-2026-0257 and authentication-override cookies/cert config are remediated. 3) Hunt: from any host reachable post-VPN, pivot to PsExec admin-share execution, C:\PerfLogs\ staging, Defender tamper, and log-clearing (other UCs in this set).

Qilin defense evasion: Microsoft Defender Real-Time Protection disabled via Set-MpPreference/registry AIInstallation High
Detects tampering that disables Defender real-time/behavior monitoring immediately before Qilin ransomware execution, either via Set-MpPreference or direct writes to the Windows Defender policy keys. Article-specific: Arctic Wolf notes attackers deliberately disable Defender Real-Time Protection prior to running the payload. Rationale: Directly implements the article's statement that operators disable Defender Real-Time Protection before ransomware; keys off the concrete Set-MpPreference flags / Defender policy registry values that persist that action.
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management/GPO rollout temporarily setting Defender policy when migrating to a third-party AV
  • IT troubleshooting AV-vs-app performance issues via Set-MpPreference
  • Software installer that disables real-time protection during setup
  • Security lab/EICAR testing on an analyst workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe","ccmexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating account and parent process; a Defender disable from a non-management, non-SYSTEM interactive user near a fresh VPN logon is high-risk. 2) Contain: re-enable real-time protection, isolate the host, and snapshot volatile state before the payload can encrypt. 3) Hunt: search the same host and lateral peers for C:\PerfLogs\ staging, PsExec admin-share execution, event-log clearing, and the `*` + six-letter Run-key persistence value.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Windows Defender"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableAntiSpyware","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableOnAccessProtection","DisableScanOnRealtimeEnable")
| where RegistryValueData == "1"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "Set-MpPreference" and CommandLine has_any ("DisableRealtimeMonitoring","DisableBehaviorMonitoring","DisableIOAVProtection","DisableOnAccessProtection"))
    or CommandLine has_any ("sc stop WinDefend","net stop WinDefend","Uninstall-WindowsFeature Windows-Defender")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows event-log clearing (wevtutil/Clear-EventLog/1102) as Qilin anti-forensics AIInstallation High
Hunts comprehensive event-log clearing that Qilin affiliates run to remove forensic evidence, via wevtutil cl, PowerShell Clear-EventLog, or the 1102/104 audit-log-cleared events. Article-specific: Arctic Wolf calls out 'comprehensive log-clearing routines' as a consistent operational pattern. Rationale: Targets the concrete anti-forensic commands (wevtutil cl / Clear-EventLog) and the 1102 audit-log-cleared event Arctic Wolf attributes to Qilin's 'comprehensive log-clearing routines'.
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing logs during troubleshooting
  • SIEM/log-forwarding agent reconfiguration that resets a channel
  • Golden-image / provisioning scripts that clear logs before sysprep
  • Backup or disk-cleanup tooling rotating event logs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which logs were cleared and by whom; correlate the 1102 timestamp with recent VPN logon and Defender-disable events on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve any remaining/forwarded logs, and disable the initiating account. 3) Hunt: because logs are gone locally, pivot to centrally forwarded telemetry for PsExec admin-share writes, C:\PerfLogs\ payloads, and Rclone/MEGA exfil across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (" cl ","clear-log"," cl/"))
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Clear-EventLog","Limit-EventLog -ClearLog",".ClearEventLog("))
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "ClearEventLog")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (1102, 104)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Account, SubjectUserName, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin Run-key persistence: value name of asterisk plus six random lowercase letters AIInstallation High
Detects the unusual Qilin autostart persistence value—an asterisk followed by exactly six randomized lowercase alphabetic characters—written under a CurrentVersion Run/RunOnce key. Highly article-specific: this exact naming convention is called out as a Qilin signature across otherwise-varied intrusions. Rationale: Encodes the exact Qilin persistence signature from the article (asterisk + six randomized lowercase letters under a Run key) as a regex on the registry value name — near-zero legitimate collision.
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare third-party app registering a Run value that happens to start with '*' (extremely uncommon)
  • Registry-auditing not enabled produces no 4657 (coverage gap, not FP) on Sentinel path
  • Datadog wildcard approximation (six single chars) matching a non-alphabetic six-char value
  • Malware unrelated to Qilin coincidentally using an asterisk-prefixed value
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the RegistryValueData to see what binary the autostart launches (likely under C:\PerfLogs\ or a temp path) and which account/process wrote it. 2) Contain: remove the Run value, quarantine the referenced payload, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep every host for the same `*`+six-letter Run value pattern to enumerate the full blast radius, then correlate to PsExec admin-share writes and Defender-tamper events.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where RegistryValueName matches regex @"^\*[a-z]{6}$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4657
| where ObjectName has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where ObjectValueName matches regex @"^\*[a-z]{6}$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ObjectName, ObjectValueName, ProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware payload staged and executed from C:\PerfLogs\ AIInstallation High
Detects executable drops and process execution from C:\PerfLogs\, the consistent Qilin ransomware staging directory identified across affiliates. Article-specific: 'staging ransomware at C:\PerfLogs\' is named as a consistent operational pattern. Rationale: C:\PerfLogs\ is an OS-created directory that normally holds no executables; execution or exe/dll writes there map directly to the article's named Qilin staging path, making it very high fidelity.
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows performance-logging tooling writing data (not executable) files to PerfLogs — filtered here by exe/dll/bin extension
  • Legitimate diagnostics package temporarily dropping a tool in PerfLogs
  • Security tooling using PerfLogs as a scratch dir
  • Admin manually placing a utility there during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 of the PerfLogs binary and check reputation; note whether it is password-protected/packed and whether execution followed Defender-disable on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the payload before encryption spreads. 3) Hunt: use the hash and the PerfLogs path to sweep all endpoints (Qilin restages the payload per host via PsExec admin shares) and check for the `*`+six-letter Run-key and log-clearing on each hit.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FolderPath has @"\PerfLogs\" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Action="ProcessExec", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, CommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FolderPath has @"\PerfLogs\" | where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".bin" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Action="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, CommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\PerfLogs\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin pre-encryption exfiltration via Rclone/FileZilla/Proton to MEGA cloud AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts data-staging-for-exfil tooling Qilin affiliates used before ransomware deployment—Rclone to MEGA, FileZilla, and Proton Drive. Article-specific: names Rclone, Proton Drive, FileZilla and MEGA as the exfil channel in double-extortion variants. Rationale: Uses the specific exfil tools (Rclone, FileZilla, Proton Drive) and MEGA destination the article ties to Qilin double-extortion, scoped so bare rclone execution alone isn't the trigger.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using Rclone for sanctioned cloud backups/migrations
  • Developer or power user with FileZilla for routine SFTP transfers
  • Personal MEGA/Proton usage on a corporate endpoint
  • Backup product bundling rclone under a different image name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","backup.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("BACKUP-SRV01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the rclone --config/remote target and transferred volume; sudden large outbound to MEGA/Proton from a server that normally never does this is high-risk. 2) Contain: block MEGA/Proton domains at egress, kill the transfer, isolate the host, and preserve the rclone config to identify the attacker's cloud account. 3) Hunt: expect ransomware to follow exfil — sweep for C:\PerfLogs\ payloads, Defender-disable, and the `*`+six-letter Run key on the same and peer hosts, and review VPN logons from the attacker IP list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "rclone.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mega","copy","sync","--config","--transfers"))
   or FileName in~ ("filezilla.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mega.nz","mega.co.nz","protondrive","proton.me")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("mega","copy","sync","--config"))
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\filezilla.exe"
   or CommandLine has_any ("mega.nz","mega.co.nz","protondrive","proton.me")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
